su-banyosu.metaTitle: SB-9K histology water bath · tissue flotation bath
su-banyosu.metaDescription: Tissue flotation water bath for histopathology and histology labs. Stretches paraffin sections on a temperature-controlled water surface; PTFE-coated reservoir, LED lighting, PID control.
su-banyosu.description: A tissue flotation water bath for histopathology labs. The matte black PTFE-coated aluminium reservoir makes translucent sections only a few microns thick stand out against a dark background, and LED illumination makes wrinkles easy to follow. A PID controller drives the silicone heater beneath the reservoir. In the simulation you can change the setpoint, watch the section flatten and pick it up on a slide.
features: PID temperature control with a digital LED display
Silicone heater beneath the reservoir, on a heat transfer plate
Secondary safety thermostat protecting the heater

sections.heading: What is a tissue flotation bath?
body: A tissue flotation bath sits between the microtome and the slide in a histopathology lab. Paraffin sections cut at 3–5 µm compress and wrinkle during sectioning. Floated on water held a little below the melting point of the paraffin, the wax softens and the section relaxes flat, ready to be picked up on a slide.

It differs from a general laboratory water bath in what it is for: a general bath keeps tubes and samples at a set temperature, while a flotation bath works at the water surface. That is why the SB-9K reservoir is matte black and lit from inside: the translucent section and its wrinkles stand out clearly against the dark background.

sections.heading: How is it used?
steps: Fill the reservoir with fresh distilled water to at least two thirds of its depth and let it reach the setpoint.
Before sectioning, sweep dust and leftover paraffin off the water surface.
Lower the ribbon from the microtome gently onto the water, keeping it parallel to the surface; sudden movements can fold it.
The section expands within seconds. Use the LED lighting to watch the wrinkles disappear.
Dip the slide at a slight angle, bring it under the section and lift it out slowly with the section on it.

sections.heading: Choosing the water temperature
body: Keep the water below the melting point of your paraffin; the right value depends on the type of paraffin. Too cool and the section stays wrinkled; too warm and the wax melts and the section may break apart.
sections.note: These are general guidelines; your laboratory's own protocol takes precedence.

sections.heading: Installation
items: Place the bath next to the microtome, within reach without leaving your seat.
Keep it out of draughts from air conditioning, open windows and fume hoods: air moving across the surface cools the water and upsets temperature control.
Choose a bench out of direct sunlight.
Use an earthed socket; on lines with large voltage swings an external regulator is recommended.

sections.heading: Cleaning and care
items: Sweep paraffin debris off the surface after each block or case batch so that material from one sample does not carry over to the next.
Empty the water at the end of the day and dry the reservoir with a soft cloth. Water left overnight builds up biofilm.
Clean the reservoir with soapy water or a mild, non-abrasive, pH-neutral detergent.
Do not use bleach, strong acids, steel wool or abrasive powders: they scratch the PTFE coating and corrode metal parts.
To descale, add about 10% white vinegar or a citric-acid descaler, hold at 40 °C for an hour, then rinse thoroughly.
Unplug the bath before cleaning. Never fill the reservoir with flammable liquids such as alcohol, acetone or xylene.

faq.q: Is a tissue flotation bath the same as a general laboratory water bath?
faq.a: No. A general water bath keeps tubes and samples at a set temperature. A tissue flotation bath is designed to stretch paraffin sections on the water surface: the dark reservoir and the lighting make the section visible.

faq.q: Why does the section stay wrinkled or break apart?
faq.a: If it stays wrinkled, the water is not warm enough to soften the paraffin. If it breaks apart, the water is too warm. Set the temperature from the melting point of your paraffin: 44–50 °C for paraffin melting at 56–58 °C, 38–42 °C for paraffin melting at 52–54 °C.

faq.q: How do I change the setpoint?
faq.a: Press SET, then use ▲ and ▼ to change the setpoint in 0.1 °C steps; hold a key to speed up. After a few seconds the display returns to the measured water temperature.

faq.q: What happens if the water runs low?
faq.a: The secondary thermostat monitoring the heater cuts power when the heater reaches about 150 °C, and the bath will not heat until the heater cools down. The controller may keep its heating light on meanwhile. Always keep the reservoir at least two thirds full.
Fresh distilled water. Hard tap water leaves scale on the heater and slows heating. Empty the bath at the end of each day.

faq.q: Does the bath have a lid, a circulation pump or a timer?
faq.a: No. The SB-9K is designed for stretching sections at the water surface; heat comes from a silicone heater beneath the reservoir.

sections.heading: What is digital pathology?
body: In digital pathology, the tissue section on a glass slide is scanned at high resolution with a slide scanner. The result is called a whole-slide image (WSI). The pathologist examines the section on screen rather than at the microscope: panning, zooming and annotating, while the image can be archived and shared with a colleague.

AhtaPatolog is the software side of that workflow. It opens and organises scanned slides and gives the pathologist the tools for the review. Scanning slides requires a slide scanner; AhtaPatolog works with the scanned images.

sections.heading: What AhtaPatolog does
items: Opens whole-slide images in the browser, with 2× to 40× objective buttons, a minimap and a scale bar.
Region annotation with polygons and rectangles.
Distance between two points and the area of an annotated region, computed from the slide's real pixel size in µm.
Case and slide management: uploaded slides and their annotation counts in one gallery.
Side-by-side comparison of two slides with synchronised navigation.

sections.heading: Supported file formats
body: SVS (Aperio), NDPI (Hamamatsu) and TIFF-based whole-slide images.

sections.heading: Workflow
steps: Slides are scanned on a slide scanner.
The images are uploaded to AhtaPatolog and listed in the gallery.
The pathologist pans, zooms, and annotates and measures the regions that matter.
Where needed, two slides are examined side by side at the same position.

No. Distance and area measurements are tools computed from the slide's pixel size; the assessment is made by the pathologist.
AhtaPatolog is in development. You can request a demo through the contact form.

faq.q: Which scanners does it work with?
faq.a: Scanners that produce whole-slide images in SVS, NDPI or TIFF format. If you use a different format, get in touch.

faq.q: Do I need a slide scanner?
faq.a: Yes. AhtaPatolog is software that works with scanned images; scanning the slides requires a slide scanner.

faq.q: Is the viewer on this page a real slide?
faq.a: Yes, it is a real whole-slide image. The viewer shows part of AhtaPatolog's toolset; annotations you make are not sent anywhere.

about.heading: About
about.lead: Ahtapot Medical Technologies is a medical device company founded by a physician. Our aim is to design and build in Türkiye the medical devices that are sourced from abroad today.
about.body: We develop the mechanics, electronics and software of each device ourselves. Because the design knowledge stays with us, we never wait on anyone to change a part, add a feature or ship an update.
